questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't "we have a framework and a committee" sufficient evidence that a governance program is working?
options: Because frameworks and committees are inherently useless
Because committees automatically dissolve themselves after one year
Because the structures can exist on paper without anyone checking whether they're actually producing better outcomes -- having the structure isn't the same as the structure working
Because only Salesforce-certified consultants are allowed to judge governance programs
questions.explain: The lesson extends Lesson 5's point about data-quality metrics to the whole program: structures can be stood up and still not be improving anything if no one measures the outcomes.

questions.q: Which example does this lesson give as a 'Technology' pillar gap -- a control that exists on paper but isn't actually providing protection?
options: A classification scheme with no picklist values
A governance committee with too many members
A retention policy that is reviewed too frequently
Standard Duplicate Rules sitting inactive in Setup, making a report of 'Duplicate Rules configured: yes' misleading if they were never activated
questions.explain: This directly echoes Lesson 4's finding that Duplicate Rules must be deliberately activated -- a configured-but-inactive rule gives a false sense of protection if reported without noting activation status.

questions.q: What is the key difference this lesson draws between activity metrics and outcome metrics?
options: Activity metrics count governance work performed (meetings held, policies written) and are easy to count but don't prove anything improved; outcome metrics measure actual change in quality, risk, or compliance over time
There is no real difference between them
Activity metrics can only be tracked by external auditors
Outcome metrics are always less reliable than activity metrics
questions.explain: The lesson warns that leading a program report with activity counts (meetings held) without reporting what changed as a result is reporting effort, not success -- outcome metrics are the harder but more honest measure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say speed-to-resolution is an important metric in its own right?
options: Because Salesforce charges extra fees for slow incident resolution
Because it has no real value compared to other metrics

Because a mature program should be able to resolve an incident like the Meridian case study faster over successive incidents, as structural fixes start paying off -- a program resolving its tenth incident as slowly as its first hasn't actually matured
Because speed-to-resolution is only relevant to Setup Audit Trail
questions.explain: The lesson ties this directly to the Lesson 13 case study, arguing that a program's maturity should show up as a shrinking resolution time across successive similar incidents, not just more documentation.

questions.q: How does this lesson suggest using the course's own fourteen lessons?
options: Only as material for the final exam, with no further practical use
As a checklist that applies only to healthcare organizations
As a list of topics to forget once the final test is passed

As a practical maturity checklist for assessing any real Salesforce org's governance program -- named owners, active and measured quality controls, a followed retention policy, working compliance processes, driven classification, traceable audits, and a maintained framework with a functioning committee
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly repurposes the course's own lesson sequence as a real-world maturity checklist, tying each lesson's topic to a concrete yes/no-with-evidence question about a real org.
